## [§5.3.b] Trial with penalty — definition and logic

I call it a trial. with penalty. That sounds ugly. That's how I' call it internally. You wouldn't say that to somebody. But it's a trial with penalty. So basically, a customer can try out your product or service for free so long as they meet your terms. For comparison, the win-your-money-back offer, the attraction offer, gives customers the chance to get their money back if they meet the terms. In a trial with penalty offer, customers only pay if they don't meet the terms. So the win-your-money-back and the free trial with penalty are virtually the same offer; we're just changing when they pay and how they pay. So they'll mirror the actions and results that you used in win-your-money-back, but this time, we use avoiding fees rather than winning your money back as the incentive for adherence. So they avoid penalties rather than get or losing their money that they paid originally. All right, so with a trial with penalty, this isn't, "Here's my thing, see if you like it." It's, "Here's my thing. You get it for free so long as you do this stuff, which makes you a perfect fit for my next offer. And if you don't, then you have to pay for it." So it's kind of like a win-win for you, because if they don't do it, then they pay. And if they do do it, then they're gonna be really likely to buy the next thing. Now, I'm gonna give you something like, "Wait, so if they don't do it, then they pay, and they didn't wanna pay originally?" I'll cover how to get around that weirdness. Let's say you normally close three out of 10 people on your attraction offer, and now you downsell another four on a trial with penalty. Then, after the trial finishes, you upsell three of them. So you go from three sales to six sales, which doubles your customers. I use this as a downsell, but it could also be used as a front end. So I don't prefer to advertise this; I prefer to present this after someone already said no to giving me money. Some people advertise this as how they get customers. It's up to you. Obviously, that HR company advertised it as how they get customers. So if you really wanna help people, convincing them to put some skin in the game is a great way to do it. And so one of my sales rules is that everyone buys something who's qualified. And so I love that as a concept. It's like everyone should buy. Like, if they're qualified and we have the thing, every person should buy. The terms may change, but everyone should buy. So, here's the difference between trials and penalties and rebates. A trial is they j- you just get a card and then bill them later. A penalty/incentive is you get a card and bill later and also if they don't complete their activation activities. So the fees are associated with non-consumption and not showing up to other sales consultations. Remember the four things we had in the win-your-money-back is you wanna have them advertise your business, you wanna have them show up for sales consults, you wanna do things that, um, that get them results, and... There's another one. I can't remember what it was, but there's four, and those are the main ones. All right? So you want to associate them doing the things that gets them results, because if they get results, then they'll probably wanna buy. All right? So they're not here' for a trial; they're here to solve a problem, so solve it, because trials don't do anything. Them taking action is just what's going to solve their problem. And if someone has a problem with that, it's an easy thing to get around. Think about the logic. If someone says, "I'm not willing to commit to that," you're like, "Well, do you want the outcome?" They're gonna say yes. It's like, "Well, you have to do this stuff to get the outcome." So if you don't, if you don't plan on doing this stuff, then you're never going to get the outcome. This is just the easiest way that I can give you all this service for free. If you really do wanna do this, "I do wanna do this," great, then you're not gonna pay anything, 'cause you're gonna follow through, and this just gives you added incentive to do it. And if this doesn't work for you, then certainly nothing else will.

## [§7.1.b] The 5-step build process (attraction → upsell → downsell → continuity → stack)

So let's go through steps for making your own. So step one is you start with an attraction offer. It al- always starts with getting people to engage, getting leads to engage with you. Step two is you pick an upsell offer. You figure out, okay, the people have come in. They're coming off win-your-money-back. They're coming on, uh, buy X get Y free. They're coming on, uh, decoy offer. Whatever it is, they're coming on the front end. You say, "Great, now I'm either gonna do a menu upsell, I'm gonna do an anchor- anchor upsell, I'm gonna do a rollover upsell." All of those things you can use as your second, second piece. Then you can pick your downsell offer. So what if they say no to any of these other offers? Well, we have our. entire downsell flow, which is we start with payment plans, uh, then we do a free trial, or we do payment plan to feature downsell. Then we go to free trial. You just pick the ones that you know that you can execute on right? now. Step four, then you' pick a continuity offer. And the result is. that you get your cash back in 30 days, more customers, and make more money.

So we just finished all of the continuity offers, continuity bonuses, continuity discounts, and the weave fee offer, which leads us to making your money model. So it is now your turn. Remember, there's document, demonstrate, duplicate. This is where I turn. it over to you, where you, need to combine these things in such a way that you can maximize the amount of money that you make in the first 30 days, so you can profitably acquire customers and scale. So let's do a quick putting it all together. So overview. A money model, attraction offer, upsells, downsells, continuity. We have covered all four. If you are starting out, just pick one of the money models to inspire you to do something in your business. All right? If you're more advanced, you can start weaving two together. There are no rules for this. You can stack these. So you absolutely can do an attraction offer that you use as an upsell offer in your business. You can use a continuity offer on the front to attract customers. All of these things are possible. I try to present them in this way in the most logical format that I have tended to use them in my business. But there are no rules in business, as long as it is legal. So I leave that to you. All right, examples. So this is my fitness offer. So I tried to conceptualize this for you. So okay, on the front end, I ran a win-your-money-back offer. Then we would upsell, from a service perspective, for anybody who bought that, we'd upsell buy X get Y- Y free. So this would be them pre-paying time. And then we would upsell the continuity bonus. Great. So that would be the rollover upsell. Now, if someone, uh, didn't wanna do win-your-money-back, then we would downsell the free trial with penalty, and then we would use the menu upsell in terms of supplements, and then we'd do the rollover upsell on the back end. And so this was fundamentally the money model. So I used one, two, three, four, five of the offers that I talked about to make the money model that we had for fitness. This model was superior to other models on the market, which is why our gyms consistently out-compete other gyms in the marketplace. All right, so this is Gym Launch's model. So we used a decoy offer, that was the strategy call, that was the, uh, you could also consider it a free with consumption, uh, depending on how you wanna see it. But we had that offer. Then we did a classic upsell. Then we did the money- menu upsell on the back end into what level of service they wanted for the extended period of time. Did you want these other services that went with, uh, Gym Launch? Or sorry, Gym Legacy, which was the back end that we had. So some people opted for the highest version. Some people said, "You know what? I don't need, like, agency services. I just want the ads. Like, you don't have to run them. Hey, uh, but I do want you to, uh, train my sales team." And so we would basically menu upsell the features that we thought would be best for them. Now, if people didn't take the offer, we had a payment plan, feature downsell, free trial, right? And so this, so this is one, two, three, four, five, six, six of the structures that I went over for this presentation is what created the Gym Launch money model. Now, uh, newsletter and consulting. So I just love this money model. It's just, like, one of my favorite ones, uh, 'cause I mentioned it, uh, during this video, uh, training a couple times. But this was an attraction offer which was a free trial. But you're like, "Wait, how could you use a free trial as an attraction offer?" Yes, there are no rules. So we used a free trial as the attraction offer. The thing that made it cash flow was the pay less now, pay more later option of saying, "Hey, we'll get you the past newsletters." And technically, this was combined with a lifetime lower rate. So this is a continuity discount and a pay less, pay less now, pay more later, put together as one. This was the thing that got them to engage. So free trial start, 3.99 a month. Oh wait, let' me give you two years of newsletters today, and give you this discount if you choose to skip your trial. And then, of course, the, uh, the back end on that one was, uh, the business, you know, upsell consulting and things like that. If it were me, this is just that- that particular business, if it were me, I would do buy X get Y free here. So now that I've got the continuity, I would then say, "Great, now that you're in continuity, if you buy seven, I'll give you five." And then I can front load even more cash. Now, if- if I know that people stay on average two years, then I wouldn't do that, 'cause that would lose me money. But if people stay, let's say, on average, another three months, then it makes sense to do buy six get six, 'cause I still double LTV and get that cash up front. So these were actually my original notes. So I, I wanted to show you how mine actually looked. Um, and I've changed some of the names, uh, to make them a little bit more, like, friendly. Uh, but this is actually what it looked like in terms of how I would design, uh, the money models. And so the possibilities really are endless.

## [§5.3.f] Tweaking + naming + when to use vs pay-less-now

A couple other tidbits. So to tweak, tweak your trial to get the most customers. If no one takes your trial, lower the requirements or the priorities. If people take your trial but don't follow through, emphasize explaining how the fees help them, and make sure that you include meetings as mandatory. Like you have to highlight it. That's why I have the little separate lines for them to initial, and I walk through it with them. Don't let them read it. Explain each one, get them to nod, then initial. All right? If people don't stay on the back end, better emphasize the value of staying and paying. That's the early part where I said, "Hey, if we get you the results, would you stay?" We added that back in to our scripting when I saw my guys weren't doing it and we weren't getting as many ascensions. We added it back in, and then way more trials started ascending. Let people make up for goofs. So people often get discouraged after getting billed. But you can offer the opportunity to make it up. So this does a great job of getting people back on track and converting. But if they miss that, you're justified in billing them. So I don't see... Like if you, they miss something, you reach out, you reach out again. You say, "Hey, I'll make it..." You know, "I'll, I'll waive it, just come back in." If they miss the next one, it's up to you. I usually don't, but that, I just think that is a completely, you're completely justified in billing at that point. In terms of naming, just call it a trial. Just say, "We do it in a special way. And the way we do it gets people results rather than, than not results." That's pretty much it. So even though the trial with penalty has some special features, you should just call it a trial. Um, otherwise people may get scared or confused and no one wants to be penalized. All right? And if they ask you why you do free trials this way, just reply with, "It's how we've always done it." Pay less now, uh, or pay more later versus trial with penalty. So I use pay less now or pay more later as a downsell for physical products or one-time services. I use trial with penalty as a downsell for recurring products or services. Also, I've only made this work in businesses where the customer has to do work to get results. So if you find other types of businesses that this works for, these trials where they don't have to do anything, let me know. For the most part though, it's usually when somebody has to do something. Oftentimes like software, you usually have to do a lot of stuff in the software. Services, it's common for customers to have to do a bunch of stuff. Um, that's more, that's more normal.... discounts, uh, get card on file. So some people get weird when you offer free stuff and then ask for a card. And if you have a super low price, it justifies the card. So a small price, uh, means the card will probably work when automatic payments start. So instead of a free month, you might offer a firth month for a first month for a dollar, or then X dollars per month when it recurs. And so if you want, you can offer for a buck, a dollar down, $10 down, whatever, um, if you have a hard time with it. Anybody who has any acumen in sales should never have an issue closing a free trial with a card, personally. Rebates are a little tougher, uh, but they work the same way. You just get them to pay up front. So I consider rebates similar to win-your-money-back, but usually for smaller, like smaller in scope. So just get them to do the thing you need them to do, and then they get the rebate. So that was kind of like the, the story that I gave with, uh, Layla. So she paid, you know, 500 bucks. She had to attend two webinars or three webinars. Very clear, very small, very straightforward. That's where rebates are kind of nice, um, rather than, you know, billing. Because the thing is, is the rebate, you know the card works because you, they paid for it and then they get it rebated, which is basically a rollover onto their service afterwards. So those are the, uh, important points. Quick summary. In a trial with penalty offer, customers can try our product or service for free so long as they meet your terms. Trial with penalties, downsell offers get yeses from people who would have said no. To do them, you get the card, get the commitment, explain why they have to do it to get the results, the meetings they have to attend and what happens if they don't do it, and use the same refund criteria from your win-your-money-back, the attraction offer number one, to create your trial with penalty criteria. This way, at the end of the trial, they've done the stuff that makes a great tr- long-term customer, and they advertise your business for you. Breakup fees, you can charge by criteria or you can charge a lump fee. I like breaking them up. So you can either say, "It's $50 for each of these occurrences." Or you can just say, "If you mess up any of these, you pay the full boat." I prefer the small dings, because then people are like, "Oh, I missed one. Now I shouldn't even try," right? I don't like that. You make money by getting people results and turning them into customers, not nickel-and-diming them with fees. My personal opinion. So use mid-trial check-ins to make more offers. If they love it, give them more of what they love. If they have problems, swap it for what makes sense for them. If they aren't using it, offer the ability to make it up to avoid the fees. This style of trial converts as much or a much higher percentage on the back end, which is why I do them. It retains goodwill, because you actually look like you're trying to help, which you are, and you get agreement before explaining the fees, just as a quick reminder, 'cause it's super important. And you can always do a normal trial as a down-downsell and remove that. But at that point, I don't think that person really is... They're just trying to leave. Um, and remember, everyone buys something. That's free trials.

## [§5.3.a] How I learned it — HR platform rebate story

All right, so we just completed payment plan downsells, and if you get to the end of the seven steps and someone's like, "I still don't wanna pay you," or, "I still don't have the money," either way, you can offer a free trial. And I've run a lot of free trials in my life, and I think there's a wrong way, to do them and a better way to do them. And I will explain the better way. So same vibe as always, let's break down how I learned this puppy. So, um, we were scaling Gym Launch, and we needed a HR platform. And Leila was looking at all these different platforms, and she ended up going with this one. And, uh, I was like, "Well, what made you, you know, pick that platform versus the other?" She was like, "Honestly, they were all more or less the same, but these guys said they'd charge me 500 bucks, and if I attended the two or three training sessions, they would rebate me the $500. But if I didn't attend the onboarding and training sessions, they would keep it. And so, of course, I attended the sessions, and now I know how to use their software, and I don't feel like learning anyone else's." And so they actually got a customer and we stayed with that platform for years because of a really interesting way of basically doing a free trial. Now, theirs was they charged and then did a rebate. But I saw the structure and was like, "Ooh, this is really interesting." And so I was like, "What if we did trials like this?" And so that's what we started doing. And so
